payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image visibly use a chalk-like medium or treatment, rather than merely showing generic blur, grain, or softened photographic detail?
node.criteria: pass: identifiable chalk-like marks or surface behavior are visible, beyond generic grain, blur, or softened photographic detail; fail: the image clearly lacks such chalk-like treatment; unknown: the visible evidence does not distinguish chalk-like treatment from generic filtering.
node.binding: Assess only visible evidence of chalk-like medium or treatment. Do not assess whether the image is a drawing or whether the conversion covers the whole scene.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image has a visibly chalk-like, dusty textured surface with softened, sketch-like outlines and smudged shading, beyond ordinary photographic detail.
The edited image has a visibly chalk-like, dusty surface with broad smudged strokes and sketchy outlines, beyond generic blur or grain.
The edited image has a visibly chalk-like, dusty surface with textured, sketchy marks across the scene, beyond generic blur or softened photographic detail.

The edited image has a visibly chalk-like, dusty surface with softened, sketchy outlines and textured shading across the scene, beyond ordinary photographic grain or blur.

n3: The node’s binding is too underspecified: it asks whether the image became a chalk drawing but does not make the two distinct requirements and the partial-progress rule operational. Clarify that the saved supports must be combined without treating a chalk-like texture alone as proof of drawing conversion, or a drawing-like rendering alone as proof of chalk medium. In particular, when one support affirms chalk-like treatment and the other reports retained photographic detail/no clear drawing conversion, preserve that affirmative progress as partial; do not promote it to complete merely because both cues are described positively elsewhere. The traces vary between complete and partial on similar support evidence, suggesting the criterion needs a stable distinction between genuine scene-wide drawing conversion and surface effects over photo-like content. Conversely, do not treat a failed drawing cue by itself as proof of no progress. Keep the existing evidence-only and unrelated-edit safeguards. All traces are valid, queried, and dependency-complete, so this is semantic criterion/binding ambiguity, not a transport or schema failure; confidence variation is a signal to clarify the rule, not evidence that the edit is absent.
n2: Make the binding explicitly operational for this node’s single criterion: judge whether substantial scene content has genuinely been redrawn, distinguishing changed forms/shading and drawn contours across the scene from photographic detail merely softened or covered with grain/texture. Keep chalk-medium assessment out of this support. The edited image retains recognizable giraffe and scene detail but has conspicuous sketch-like outlines and simplified, painterly treatment, so avoid treating either cue alone as decisive; record the drawing-conversion evidence without implying the separate chalk requirement is satisfied. Preserve uncertainty when the visual evidence cannot distinguish conversion from filtering, and do not infer overall completion or no progress from this support alone. The traces are valid and dependency-complete, so address semantic criterion consistency—not transport/schema issues. Their pass/fail variation is a reason to clarify the evidence threshold, not proof that the requested edit is absent.
